accepted.question_text: A pure O-sequence is the h-vector of a pure monomial order ideal, where all maximal monomials have the same degree; its type is the number of maximal monomials. What is the largest type t for which every pure O-sequence is unimodal, without imposing any restriction on codimension or socle degree? In particular, does unimodality always hold for pure O-sequences of type 2?

evidence.quote: A monomial order ideal, X, is called pure if all maximal monomials of X (in the partial ordering given by divisibility) have the same degree. A pure O-sequence is the h-vector of a pure monomial order ideal. For reasons that will be clear shortly, we call e the socle degree of h. The type of a pure O-sequence is the number of maximal monomials.

What is the largest type t for which all pure O-sequences are unimodal (independently of the codimension or socle degree)? Even proving that t >= 2, i.e., that pure O-sequences of type 2 are unimodal in any codimension, would be very interesting.

accepted.question_text: A pure O-sequence is the h-vector of a pure monomial order ideal, and codimension is the number of variables in the ambient polynomial ring. For a fixed codimension r, what is the largest type t for which every pure O-sequence of codimension r is unimodal?
accepted.context_brief: Unimodality threshold by codimension and type

evidence.quote: A pure O-sequence is the h-vector of a pure monomial order ideal.
Without loss of generality we will assume that I does not contain nonzero linear forms, so we will define r to be the codimension of A.
For a fixed codimension r, what is the largest type t for which all pure O-sequences are unimodal?

accepted.question_text: A pure O-sequence is the h-vector of a pure monomial order ideal; its socle degree is the common degree of the maximal monomials, and codimension is the number of variables. For a fixed codimension r, what is the largest socle degree e for which every pure O-sequence of codimension r and socle degree e is unimodal?
accepted.context_brief: Unimodality threshold by codimension and socle degree

evidence.quote: A pure O-sequence is the h-vector of a pure monomial order ideal. For reasons that will be clear shortly, we call e the socle degree of h.
Without loss of generality we will assume that I does not contain nonzero linear forms, so we will define r to be the codimension of A.
For a fixed codimension r, what is the largest socle degree e for which all pure O-sequences are unimodal?

accepted.question_text: What is the smallest codimension r for which there exists a nonunimodal pure O-sequence of socle degree 4?

evidence.quote: A pure O-sequence is the h-vector of a pure monomial order ideal. For reasons that will be clear shortly, we call e the socle degree of h.
What is the smallest codimension r for which there exists a nonunimodal pure O-sequence of socle degree 4?

accepted.question_text: Let #P(*, e, t) denote the number of pure O-sequences of socle degree e and type t. For fixed e, determine the asymptotic behavior of #P(*, e, t) as t becomes large; in particular, what is the correct order of magnitude of #P(*, e, t)?

evidence.quote: We now consider a slightly different asymptotic enumeration question. Fix positive integers e and t. Since the number of monomials dividing t monomials of degree e is finite, there are only finitely many pure O-sequences of socle degree e and type t. Denote their set by P(*, e, t).
Determine asymptotically the number #P(*, e, t) of pure O-sequences of socle degree e and type t, for t large. What is the order of magnitude of #P(*, e, t)?

accepted.question_text: A pure f-vector is the rank vector of a pure simplicial complex, equivalently a pure O-sequence generated by squarefree monomials. What is the smallest number of variables n, equivalently the smallest number of vertices of the underlying simplicial complex, for which a nonunimodal pure f-vector can exist?
accepted.context_brief: Minimum variables for nonunimodal pure f-vectors

evidence.quote: In particular, if we define as pure those simplicial complexes whose facets have all the same dimension, then clearly their rank vectors, called pure f-vectors, are the special subset of pure O-sequences that can be generated by squarefree monomials.
What is the smallest number of variables n (i.e., the number of vertices of the complex) allowing the existence of a nonunimodal pure f-vector?

accepted.question_text: A matroid can be identified with a pure simplicial complex whose restriction to any subset of the vertex set is also pure. For such matroid complexes, are the face vectors (f-vectors) always unimodal, or even log-concave? What about the corresponding h-vectors?

evidence.quote: A finite matroid can be naturally identified with a pure simplicial complex over V = {1, 2, . . . , r}, such that its restriction to any subset of V is also a pure complex.

Stanley's Twenty-Fifth Problem for the year 2000 IMU Volume "Mathematics: frontiers and perspectives" [70] asks, among a few other things: are all matroid f-vectors unimodal, or even log-concave? What about matroid h-vectors?

accepted.question_text: If Delta is a matroid complex and S/I_Delta is its Stanley-Reisner ring, is the h-vector of S/I_Delta always a pure O-sequence?

evidence.quote: It is a standard fact of combinatorial commutative algebra (see e.g. [69]) that the Stanley-Reisner ring S/I∆ of a matroid complex is Cohen-Macaulay and level, although of course of positive Krull-dimension (except in degenerate cases). Thus, the h-vector of S/I∆ is level, since it is the h-vector of an artinian reduction of S/I∆.
Conjecture 3.4. Any matroid h-vector is a pure O-sequence.

accepted.question_text: Does every complete intersection have the Weak Lefschetz Property, meaning that multiplication by a general linear form has maximal rank in the case d = 1?
accepted.context_brief: Weak Lefschetz property for complete intersections

evidence.quote: When I is an arbitrary artinian homogeneous ideal, the above maximal rank property for all d and i is called the Strong Lefschetz Property (SLP), and the case d = 1 is called the Weak Lefschetz Property (WLP).

As a trivial example, we know that monomial complete intersections in any codimension possess the WLP, thanks to Theorem 2.3. It is not known (except in codimension <= 3, as noted below) whether all complete intersections have this property, but the knowledge in the special case of monomial ideals is enough to say that all complete intersection Hilbert functions are unimodal.

accepted.question_text: For the class of pure O-sequences, if two sequences agree in every entry except one and the differing entries differ by a positive integer alpha, must every intermediate value also occur in a pure O-sequence? In particular, does this Interval Conjecture for Pure O-sequences remain true in three variables?

evidence.quote: Namely, the IP says that if two (not necessarily finite) sequences, h and h' , of a class S of integer sequences coincide in all entries but one, say h = (h0, . . . , hi-1, hi, hi+1, . . .) and h' = (h0, . . . , hi-1, hi + alpha, hi+1, . . .), for some index i and some positive integer alpha, then the sequences (h0, . . . , hi-1, hi + beta, hi+1, . . .) are also in S, for all beta = 1, 2, . . . , alpha - 1.

In a more combinatorial direction, in BMMNZ 2012 the IP has then also been conjectured for: 1) pure O-sequences (under the name "ICP"); and 2) the f-vectors of pure simplicial complexes, a topic of discussion of the next section.
While the ICP remains open in most instances -- e.g., in three variables -- it must be pointed out that, just recently, it has been disproved in the four variable case by Constantinescu and Varbaro.

accepted.question_text: Classify all finite projective planes, or at least determine exactly which integers q can occur as their orders. Here a projective plane is a collection of points and lines in which any two lines intersect in exactly one point and any two points lie on exactly one line; when the plane is finite, the number of points is q^2 + q + 1 and each line contains q + 1 points.

evidence.quote: Recall that a projective plane is a collection of points and lines such that any two lines "intersect at" exactly one point, and any two points "lie on" exactly one line (one also assumes that there exist four points no three of which are collinear, in order to avoid uninteresting pathological situations).

If the projective plane is finite, it can easily be seen that the number of points is equal to the number of lines, and that this number must be of the form q^2+q+1, where the integer q is the order of the plane. Further, in a projective plane of order q, any line contains exactly q + 1 points, and by duality, any point is at the intersection of exactly q + 1 lines.
A major open problem in geometry asks for a classification of all finite projective planes, or even just of the possible values that q may assume.

accepted.question_text: Does there exist a Steiner system S(4, 5, 21), that is, a 21-element set together with a collection of 5-element blocks such that every 4-element subset is contained in exactly one block? Equivalently, is the sequence (1, 21, 210, 1330, 5985, 1197) a pure O-sequence?

evidence.quote: A Steiner system S(l, m, r) is an r-element set V , together with a collection of m-subsets of V , called blocks, such that every l-subset of V is contained in exactly one block.
The smallest value of r for which the existence of S(4, 5, r) is currently open is 21. In other words, it is unknown whether (1, 21, 210, 1330, 5985, 1197) is a pure O-sequence.
